definition: An agent conditions its action on what its partner did previously, cooperating after cooperation and retaliating after defection.
A peer pays a cost to reduce the payoff of an agent who deviated from cooperation.
Agents must prove identity and act only within delegated, bounded permissions that leave an accountable chain.
Agents voluntarily agree to enforceable, pre-specified conditional transfers or obligations.
An agent posts a deposit up front that is forfeited if it is found to violate the agreed rule.
A hard ceiling limits how often a single agent may take an action or draw on a shared resource in a time window.
Agents give help to others depending on the recipients' reputation from past conduct toward third parties.
Agents (or a manager) may reward cooperators and penalize deviators, with both instruments available.
A shared, persistent record of agents' past behavior is available to future counterparts.
Agents can voluntarily lock themselves into a declared future action or plan before others move.
A package of community governance principles (boundaries, local rules, collective choice, monitoring, graduated sanctions, dispute resolution, nesting) evaluated together.
Agents pay a charge proportional to the harm their actions impose on others, internalizing the externality.
Each repeated deviation triggers a more severe response than the last.
Norms are written as explicit obligations and prohibitions that a central controller monitors and enforces.
Group members vote on and adopt the rules or sanctions that will govern them.
An allocation and payment rule is designed so that truthful reporting is each agent's best strategy.
Agents infer the group's norms by observing which behaviors others sanction or approve.
A monitor inspects messages or internal states exchanged between agents to detect covert coordination.
Agents announce intended actions before interacting without any enforcement of the announcement.
Agents choose whether to join an institution in which contributions are enforced by sanctions.
Agents themselves assign reputation scores to others from local observation, and these scores shape rewards.
A deviating agent is excluded or expelled from the group or system.
An agent who reports a collusive agreement it belongs to receives leniency or a reward.
Agents reduce their own use of a shared resource when they detect congestion signals.
Agents cut their link to a partner who deviated and interact with others instead.
Agents pass information about others' conduct to third parties who might interact with them.
Agents' actions are recorded in a log that cannot be altered undetectably and is attributable to the actor.

code: visibility of individual conduct to peers
definition: Each agent's conduct is identifiable and observable by peers.
A central planner learns and adjusts rewards and penalties paid to agents to steer them toward cooperation.
Sanctioned agents can contest an enforcement decision through a review process run by the enforcer.
Each agent carries a persistent identifier linking it to a responsible party so counterparts and investigators can act on it.
Designated auditors check agents' tamper-evident action logs against expected behavior to expose faults with verifiable evidence.
A staged protocol governs authorization, execution and accounting of payments between untrusted agents.
Audits of agent behavior are scheduled selectively to maximize detection under a fixed monitoring budget.
The community collectively reverses or overrides an outcome produced by the formal rules.
An excluded or suspended agent can regain membership by meeting specified conditions.
Decisions require consensus, and a qualified member's justified objection blocks the decision.
Agent interactions are confined to a bounded environment with controlled permeability to the outside.
Agents earn credit for providing service to others and spend credit to obtain service themselves.
Interaction with a counterpart is suspended automatically once its failures exceed a threshold, with periodic trials to resume.
Payment is held by a neutral mechanism and released only when the counterpart's performance is confirmed.
Penalty severity is set in relation to the probability of detection to deter deviation at least cost.
A group is held jointly responsible for any member's default, giving members reason to monitor and pressure each other.
Equals check in on and hold each other to account without a formal authority.
A body independent of the rule-maker hears appeals of enforcement decisions and issues binding rulings.
Compliance is verified through inspection or testing of agents' conduct.
Messages are tagged with their origin so receivers can distinguish agent-originated content from authoritative instructions.
A standard, easy-to-find channel lowers the cost of reporting problems to the responsible party.
Agents must complete prescribed verification steps before taking consequential actions.
The group elects the agent who monitors compliance, lending the monitor legitimacy.
Higher-tier rules, harder to change, govern how lower-tier operational rules are made.
Agents can discuss freely before or between decisions.
Agents choose among competing potential partners, so cooperation terms are set by supply and demand.
Agents form or sever relationships based on others' reputations.
Agents contribute to the community without direct exchange, expecting others to contribute in turn.
Agents who fail to punish deviators are themselves punished.
The probability or size of a penalty is adjusted to the detected degree of deviation.
Each action carries a small cost that is negligible for normal use but prohibitive for abusive volume.
Agents may unilaterally exit a commitment by paying a penalty fixed in advance.
Agents are instructed to reason about the social consequences of their actions before acting.
Agents identify which institution is authoritative and follow and enforce only its rules.
A moderator removes contributions that violate the community's rules.
Designers remove conflicting options from agents' action sets before interaction.
Agents receive a fixed reward for each contribution the system accepts.
Strategies that earn more spread in the population through selection or imitation.
Code-based contracts automatically execute registration, allocation and bookkeeping rules among agents.
A third party maintains a list of known deviators that others use to refuse interaction.
Agents sign an attributable statement certifying that their contribution complies with the rules.
Peers express disapproval or shame toward a deviator, imposing a non-monetary cost.
Agents hold shares in others' returns so that their own payoff rises with others' success.
Contributors are rewarded with prestige or elevated social status.

code: third party bonds agent for premium
definition: A third party posts a forfeitable bond on an agent's behalf in exchange for a premium and audit rights.
A neutral clearing party determines whether an agent met its obligation and which settlement follows.
Agents learn about others by observing interactions they are not part of.
A credible threat to impose costs is used to induce compliance before any cost is imposed.
Payoffs are redistributed among agents so that the social optimum becomes individually optimal.
A trusted monitor inspects an untrusted agent's actions and blocks or resamples suspicious ones.
A partner reduces the resources it supplies to a partner that fails to contribute.
A written code states expected conduct, with designated handlers for reported violations.
